title: Runbook Warm-Handoff and Dry-Run Catalog
author: Leila Matsumoto
content:
Runbook Warm-Handoff and Dry-Run Catalog

Short summary
This page describes a lightweight, repeatable lifecycle for runbooks and the practices we use to: 1) perform warm-handoffs between responders, 2) run scheduled dry-runs (game-day exercises) that validate runbook steps and tooling, and 3) measure readiness through a simple scoring rubric. The intent is to reduce friction during live incidents and improve runbook quality over time.

Audience and scope
- Audience: SREs, on-call engineers, incident commanders, team leads, and any engineer owning customer-facing services.
- Scope: Applies to production-facing runbooks, on-call pairing, scheduled exercises, and the templates used for internal/ external communications. This does not replace the Incident Command Playbook (see related pages) but augments it with operational readiness practices.

Objectives
- Ensure every runbook is runnable by a responder unfamiliar with the service within 30 minutes.
- Standardize warm-handoffs so context loss during rotation is minimized.
- Run at least one dry-run per service per quarter.
- Maintain a triage-to-postmortem pipeline where evidence is collected automatically during an incident.

High-level process diagram (text)
1) Runbook author creates/updates runbook -> 2) Peers review -> 3) Runbook enters roster for dry-run -> 4) Dry-run executed -> 5) Issues found are fixed; runbook updated -> 6) Runbook promoted to active roster

Roles & responsibilities
- Incident Commander (IC): drives incident lifecycle, accepts warm-handoffs, and signs off on containment/restore decisions.
- Primary Responder / Owner: service-level subject matter expert (SME), holds the runbook, performs fix actions.
- Bridge Operator: runs communication templates, updates status page, and coordinates stakeholder comms.
- Secondary / Scribe: records actions, timestamps, and evidence for the postmortem.
- Runbook Owner: maintains runbook currency and triages dry-run findings (usually the on-call owner for the service).

Incident lifecycle (concise steps)
1) Detection & Acknowledgement
   - Monitoring triggers: alerts that match alerting rules (see SLOs below). Pager duty escalation rules apply.
   - Acknowledge within 2 minutes.
2) Initial Triage (10 minutes)
   - IC or primary responder performs quick scope assessment: blast radius, customer impact, affected regions.
3) Containment (20–60 minutes)
   - Execute containment steps from the runbook (e.g., redirect traffic, scale instances, set feature flag).
4) Recovery (variable)
   - Apply fix; validate recovery with health checks and golden requests.
5) Communication & Handoff
   - If extended incident: perform warm-handoff (see protocol).
6) Post-incident: evidence collection, postmortem within 72 hours, and action triage.

Runbook lifecycle and quality gates
- Runbook frontmatter must include: service, owner, severity mapping, last-tested date, and runbook-version.
- Minimum runbook sections: Purpose, Preconditions/Assumptions, Detection steps, Containment, Recovery, Rollback, Verification, and After-action notes.
- Quality gates before promotion to active roster: peer review done, 1 successful dry-run, automated smoke-test present.

Warm-handoff protocol (chat + artifacts)
1) Precondition: IC decides to hand off or shift change occurs.
2) Handoff message (Slack): use the channel #ops-bridge-{service}. Template: 

[Handoff] Service: {service}
Time: {UTC timestamp}
IC: {name} -> New IC: {name}
Severity: {S1/S2/S3}
Current status: {contains summary}
Actions in progress: {list}
Next steps & blockers: {list}
Runbook link: {confluence link}
Evidence: {log links, grafana dashboards, traces}

3) Live Handoff checklist (must be completed in a single message or short call):
- New IC confirms they read the runbook and dashboard.
- Scribe confirms evidence links are captured.
- Bridge Operator confirms external status page message is published (if customer impact).
- Ownership recorded in incident metadata (pagerduty / incident tracker).

Dry-run (quarterly catalog)
- Cadence: Each production service is scheduled for a dry-run at least once per quarter. High-risk services (SLO > 99.95% or high revenue impact) run monthly.
- Participants: Runbook Owner, on-call pair (primary + secondary), one observer (cross-team), Bridge Operator.
- Duration: 90–120 minutes.
- Scenario types (rotate): throttling / saturation, KV-cache corruption, model-loading failure, multi-region network partition, degraded quality/regression.
- Pre-reads: runbook, runbook checklist, access credentials, and predefined dataset to validate recovery.

Dry-run script template
1) Briefing (10 min): objectives, scope, safety (no actions that can affect customers without approval).
2) Inject (15 min): simulated alert triggers; observers monitor.
3) Execute (45–60 min): follow runbook; record timings and decisions.
4) Debrief (20 min): retro on what worked, where steps were confusing, blocked actions.
5) Score and publish findings (see rubric).

Readiness scoring rubric (simple)
- Runbook accessibility (0–2): 0=not available, 1=available but incomplete, 2=complete and linked from service page.
- Runbook runnability (0–4): how many critical steps were completed without external help.
- Tooling & dashboards (0–2): dashboards present and correct.
- Handoff clarity (0–2): warm-handoff completed and accepted.
- Total: 0–10. Passing: >=7.

On-call pairing guidance
- New-to-service engineers are paired with a veteran for first two rotations (6 weeks).
- Pairing routine: daily 15-minute sync during first week, weekly check-ins thereafter.
- Pairing checklist: access validated (k8s, cloud console, runbook edit rights), runbook walkthrough completed, one supervised incident or dry-run completed.

Postmortem template (required within 72 hours)
- Title: <Service> - <Incident date> - <short summary>
- Summary (1–2 lines)
- Timeline with timestamps (UTC)
- Impact & customers affected
- Root cause analysis (do not prematurely assign blame)
- Corrective actions (owner + due date)
- Mitigations & permanent fixes
- Evidence & links (logs, dashboards, recordings)
- Learnings & follow-ups

Status page & customer communications templates
- Severity 1 (widespread outage): publish initial status within 15 minutes. Update cadence: every 20–30 minutes or when key milestones achieved.
- Severity 2 (degraded core functionality): publish initial status within 60 minutes. Update cadence: hourly.
- Severity 3 (minor or scheduled maintenance): publish initial status within 4 hours.

Status page sample (short)
- Title: Service degraded: {service} API errors
- Impact: Intermittent errors for some regions; potential partial data loss in in-flight requests
- Current status: Investigating
- Next update: {UTC timestamp +30m}

Customer email template (S1 initial)
Subject: Incident affecting {service} — we are investigating
Body:
Hello {customer_name},
We are currently investigating an issue impacting {service} which may affect {exact customer-visible symptoms}. Our engineers are actively working to restore service. We will send our next update by {timestamp}.
If you have urgent concerns, contact {support contact link}.
— Redwood Inference Support

SLOs, alert thresholds and triggers (examples)
| Metric | SLO | Alert trigger | Action |
|---|---:|---|---|
| 95th pct latency (text-gen) | 95% < 150ms | 95th > 250ms for 5m | Pager to on-call, start mitigation runbook |
| Request error rate (5m) | < 0.5% | errors > 1% for 3m | Pager to on-call, engage owner |
| Availability (1d) | 99.95% | availability < 99.9% for 30m | Escalate to IC and infra leads |

Evidence collection checklist (for postmortem)
- Grafana snapshots covering incident window.
- Kibana/ELK query results exported.
- Perf traces for representative requests.
- PagerDuty incident log and Slack bridge export.
- Runbook execution timestamps (who ran which step).

Runbook governance and versioning
- Version each runbook with semantic versioning: vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Update changelog in frontmatter.
- Every runbook must record last-tested date; if older than 180 days it is flagged for revalidation.
- Quarterly sweep by Runbook Council (2 ops + rotating engineering reps) to triage out-of-date runbooks.

Appendix A: CLI snippets and quick checks
- Recreate smoke traffic (python):
  python tools/smoke.py --service {service} --profile test --count 50
- Fetch recent traces:
  curl -s "${TRACING_URL}/api/traces?service={service}&from={start}&to={end}" | jq .

Appendix B: Example runbook frontmatter (YAML)
---
service: payments-api
owner: team-payments
severity-mapping: S1: complete-outage, S2: degraded-throughput
last-tested: 2026-08-01
runbook-version: v1.4.2
---

Appendix C: Where to find help
- Incident tracker: https://redwood.incidents.example
- Runbook index: https://confluence.redwood.example/display/oncall/Runbook+Index
- PagerDuty: https://pd.example

Next steps
- Services should add this page to their runbook frontmatter link.
- Runbook owners: schedule a dry-run within the next 60 days if you have not had one in the prior quarter.
